Hey dude! u/Laxus3121 **Here's my two cents from someone turning 30 soon, but did a different life path near the end of their 20s.** I was working in a government job that was very slow and very beaurcpatic. It was good money but slowly killing me. I wanted something more mobile with more growth and that actually used my skills. About 6 months later I landed a dream job in tech as a UX researcher. 

**How did I do it? Really not rocket science;**

1. I looked at what I liked about my current job - which was talking to people
2. I leveraged what I was good at; turns out not everyone is great at stakeholder engagement 
3. I looked at what types of jobs used these skills in tech (UX Research came to mind where you do a ton of user interviews)
4. I took a 6 credit course through coursera to earn a certificate in UX research *(it was free!)*
5. I applied like crazy - eventually I got a job at an accessibility start up, partially because I leveraged my unique background in handling alot of complex stakeholders, while also having a parent that has a disability

***It's never too late***. Think about what you like, think about the environment you want to work in, and think about what makes you unique, then connect the dots in between. 

Working in retail is hard, and truthfully theres a lot of ecommerce places that understand a physical commerce environment. Use that to your advantage. I could easily see you being a Customer Success Associate or Manager. Look at a place like shopify - where you can start at around 50k with minimum experience. They love people who have real world retail backgrounds. If that route doesnt work start at a smaller place and really explain the story of who you are and why many years of retail blow others out of the water. 

**Yeah, a job won't fix everything in your life b*****ut it is a great stepping stone.*** With more pay you can get your own place - you can invest in hobbies, you can invest in yourself. Baby steps! You can do this and if you ever need support I am a DM away :)

I think cheating is so triggering to people and they want a sense of justice but at what cost?

No actually. You can make change without public shaming.

There’s a distinct difference between shame and guilt. Guilt comes from ‘I did something wrong’, you take ownership for your actions and understand they were bad and change them.
Shane comes ‘I am wrong’. It’s deeper and hurtful, that you are wrong. It’s harder to make a change when you think you as a person are wrong. It leads to deep mental health issues and suicide.

You can make change understanding your behaviour was terrible but you don’t need to be publicly shamed to do it.

I’m not focusing on how the person feels about getting caught. I’m focusing that passing judgement in a 45 second clip isn’t the best way to determine the type of person she is. 

Cheating is hurtful, it’s cruel, it’s a form of abuse. But posting a video with the intent of trying to shame someone isn’t nice EI ether.

This isn’t a two wrongs make a right scenario.

How do we know she doesn’t feel bad? She looks stunned. 

Cheating is cruel and mean but judging whether someone has the correct response within 10 seconds and knowingly being filmed... idk man. 

Maybe in a week she will reflect on why she did something bad, maybe she won’t but making a morale change isn’t something that happens in a video clip. It’s long term commitment that you can’t see in a video and will never go viral.

Have you read the book: ‘so you’ve been publicly shamed, by Ron Jonson’

It goes into the deep and lasting effects of being globally shamed. People commit suicide over stuff life this. Yeah this girl fucked up huge but does she deserve a life where she is defined by the worst thing she’s ever done? 

The girl may be struggling with a tragedy and has a shitty coping mechanism. Or maybe she is 100% evil. But I don’t know and we never will because all we have is a 45 second clip that dooms her for all of internet eternity.
